title: Numbers 0 to 20
goal: Count from 0 to 20, pronounce the tricky numbers correctly, and catch small numbers when you hear them.

items.en: how six, dix, huit and neuf change sound before another word

drills.prompt: In which phrase does the x of six sound like a z?
drills.explain: Before a vowel sound, six and dix link with a z sound: si‿z‿euros.

drills.prompt: How do you pronounce neuf in neuf ans (nine years)?
drills.explain: Before ans and heures, the f of neuf becomes a v sound.
dix euros: the x links with a z sound, di‿z‿euros.

items.note: Alone: “seess”. Before a consonant: “see”. Before a vowel: “seez”.
Say “weet”. Never l' before it: le huit.
Works like six: “deess” alone, “dee” before a consonant, “deez” before a vowel.
Don't confuse with deux (2): douze ends with a z sound.
The g and the t are silent: it sounds like vin (wine).

blocks.title: Signing up for a French class
blocks.context: Karim registers for a free French class at a community centre in Montréal. Lucie, a volunteer, fills in the form.

lines.speaker: Lucie
lines.en: Thank you. Where do you live?

lines.speaker: Karim
lines.fr: J'habite rue Saint-Denis, au numéro six.
lines.en: I live on Saint-Denis Street, at number six.

lines.speaker: Lucie
lines.fr: Parfait. Le cours est en salle quinze. Et voici le livre. On commence à la page cinq.
lines.en: Perfect. The class is in room fifteen. And here is the book. We start on page five.

lines.speaker: Karim
lines.fr: Salle quinze, page cinq. Merci beaucoup !
lines.en: Room fifteen, page five. Thank you very much!

blocks.title: Count with Lucie
blocks.context: Lucie counts from zero to twenty. Listen once, then listen again and count along.
blocks.fr: Zéro, un, deux, trois, quatre, cinq, six, sept, huit, neuf, dix. Onze, douze, treize, quatorze, quinze, seize, dix-sept, dix-huit, dix-neuf, vingt.

blocks.body: Notice how Karim and Lucie mix up [[six]] and [[dix]], and [[deux]] and [[douze]]. Even native speakers check numbers by repeating them or saying the digits one by one, like [[un, deux]]. That is a great strategy for you too.

blocks.note: From 11 to 16, each number is one word ending in **-ze**. From 17, French adds: **dix + sept**, **dix + huit**, **dix + neuf**, joined with a **hyphen**.

blocks.title: Un or une?
blocks.body:
[[Un]] is the only number that changes for gender. Before a feminine noun it becomes [[une]]: [[un euro]], but [[une salle]] (one room). When you just count, say [[un]].

One more detail: never put [[l']] before [[huit]] or [[onze]]. Say [[le huit]], [[le onze]]. You will need this for dates.

blocks.title: Numbers in tiny contexts
blocks.note: For a house, a room, a page or an apartment, French puts the number **after** the word: [[salle quinze]], [[page cinq]]. For your address, say [[J'habite au numéro…]] (literally “I live at the number…”).

examples.fr: Le cours est en salle quinze.
examples.en: The class is in room fifteen.

examples.fr: On commence à la page cinq.

blocks.title: Six and dix have three pronunciations
blocks.body:
[[Six]] and [[dix]] are chameleons. Their last letter changes depending on what comes next:

- **Alone or at the end of a sentence:** you hear an *s*: [[six]] “seess”, [[dix]] “deess”.
- **Before a consonant:** the last letter is silent: [[six dollars]] “see dollars”, [[dix dollars]] “dee dollars”.
- **Before a vowel sound:** it links with a *z* (this is liaison, from Unit 1): [[six euros]] “see-z-euros”, [[six ans]] “see-z-an”.

[[Huit]] keeps its *t* alone and before a vowel ([[huit ans]] “wee-t-an”). Before a consonant, the *t* is traditionally silent ([[huit dollars]] “wee dollars”), but today many people pronounce it, and in dates you usually hear it: [[le huit mars]].

[[Neuf]] is special: before [[ans]] (years) and [[heures]] (hours), the *f* becomes a *v*: [[neuf ans]] “nuh-v-an”.

examples.en: two euros, three euros (liaison with z)

blocks.body:
- **Deux / douze** and **trois / treize**: the short one ends in a vowel, the long one ends with a *z* sound. Listen for that final *z*.
- **Six / seize**: [[six]] has the vowel of “see”; [[seize]] has the vowel of “said” and ends in *z*.
- **Cinq**: the *q* is pronounced, “sank”. Don't make it rhyme with English “sink”.
- **Sept**: the *p* is silent. Say “set”, not “sept”.
- **Vingt**: nothing at the end is pronounced. Say “van” with a nasal vowel.
- **Spelling 17–19**: always a hyphen: [[dix-sept]], [[dix-huit]], [[dix-neuf]].

blocks.title: Numbers in Canadian addresses
blocks.body:
In Canada, the house number comes **first**, before the street: [[6, rue Saint-Denis]]. In French-language addresses in Québec, you usually see a comma after the number.

In the Canada Post format, the apartment number comes **first**, joined to the house (civic) number with a hyphen: **12-6, rue Saint-Denis** means apartment 12 at number 6. In conversation, people usually say the house number first: [[au numéro six, appartement douze]].

Numbers above 20 come in the next lesson. Until then, if you need to give a long address number like 1250, you can read it digit by digit: [[un, deux, cinq, zéro]].

blocks.title: Listen and repeat
blocks.note: Repeat each line out loud. Pay attention to the end of six, dix and neuf.

lines.tip: douze ends with a clear z.

blocks.explain: [[seize]] ends with a z sound. [[six]] alone ends with an s sound.
[[dix euros]]: the x links with a z sound before the vowel.
[[treize]] ends with a z sound; [[trois]] ends in a vowel.
[[deux]] ends in a vowel. [[douze]] would end with a z sound.
You can write the word or the digits. In words, don't forget the hyphen: [[dix-sept]].
[[quatorze]] = 14. Words or digits are both fine here.

blocks.prompt: How do you write 18 in words?
blocks.explain: 17, 18 and 19 are dix + the number, joined with a hyphen.
optionFeedback: The order is dix first, then huit.
The two parts are joined with a hyphen, not glued together.

blocks.prompt: In “dix euros”, how does the x sound?
blocks.explain: Before a vowel sound, the x of six and dix links with a z sound: dee-z-euros.
optionFeedback: You hear s only when dix is alone.
It is silent before a consonant, as in dix dollars, but euros starts with a vowel.

blocks.explain: [[vingt]]: the g and the t are silent.

accept: La page sept, s'il vous plaît.
blocks.explain: Number after the noun: [[page sept]]. The p of sept is silent.

blocks.prompt: You are registering for a French class. Say your name, your house number (or an invented one under 20) and your apartment number. Then count slowly from 0 to 20.
checklist: Count 0 to 20, with clear douze, treize, seize

models.label: Model answer
models.fr: Je m'appelle Amira. J'habite à Montréal, au numéro dix-sept. Appartement quatre. Zéro, un, deux, trois, quatre, cinq, six, sept, huit, neuf, dix, onze, douze, treize, quatorze, quinze, seize, dix-sept, dix-huit, dix-neuf, vingt !
models.en: My name is Amira. I live in Montréal, at number seventeen. Apartment four. 0, 1, 2 … 20!

blocks.prompt: Write three short lines with numbers in words (not digits): your house number, a room number, and a page number.
checklist: Numbers written in words, with hyphens for 17–19

models.label: Model answer
models.fr: J'habite à Gatineau, au numéro dix-neuf. Le cours est en salle onze. On commence à la page seize.
models.en: I live in Gatineau, at number nineteen. The class is in room eleven. We start on page sixteen.

summary:
- Count from [[zéro]] to [[vingt]] and spell 17–19 with a hyphen
- Pronounce [[six]], [[dix]], [[huit]] and [[neuf]] correctly alone, before a consonant and before a vowel
- Tell apart [[deux/douze]], [[trois/treize]], [[six/seize]] when you hear them
- Give a house, room or page number: [[J'habite au numéro huit.]]
